event: VXE 470 was sent to the PLZ, transitioned to VTOL at about 2,400 ft AGL, ran the HLB down during the long VTOL descent and crashed into trees, destroying the center wing.
failure_mode: GCS recalculated mission waypoint MSL values from the origin point elevation instead of waypoint terrain elevation, putting the PLZ pattern about 3,200 ft above the launch point, so VTOL transition started far too high for the HLB
contributing: GCS origin placed about 24 km away at an elevation of about 16 to 23 ft
no GCS or vehicle limit on VTOL transition altitude
operator held landing pause until VTOL rejected it at low HLB
GCS 6.1.2 with non-standard gcs.ini (LzGlide=0) spamming parachute commands on the datalink

evidence.quote: The XComm log shows an MSL of 2,936' as the HOME point before launch.
The GCS/Origin point was set ~24km away at an elevation of ~16-23'.
The crux of the problem is that some code is incorrectly using the elevation of the origin point as the reference elevation.
You can see in the FDR that after the RTB is commanded the vehicle is commanded to climb from 1500' to 3000'.
Additionally, the logs show that the landing was paused until the VTOL rejected pause commands due to low HLB.

team_root_cause: GCS Software bug that calculates incorrect MSL values for mission waypoints when the origin is located at significantly different elevations.
reasoning: The XComm home point was 2,936 ft MSL while the mission table put launch at 316 ft MSL, and the GCS origin was found about 24 km away at near sea level. GCSS-352 reproduced the GCS recalculating waypoint MSL from the origin elevation, and the FDR shows the commanded altitude climbing to 3,000 ft on RTB before a high VTOL transition. The long descent then depleted the HLB and the aircraft fell.
notes: FS2-2825 is titled 'Firmware CAs (VXEP-556)' but is a clone of the VXEP-512/546 high transition epic; VXEP-556 is an unrelated W1 ticket, so the key in that title looks like a typo. The fix (GCSS-352) was pulled from 6.4 and later canceled, so the bug fix status is unclear.

event: Center wing 300 (and 689) would not mount securely to the fuselage when the wing shift bracket was fitted, leaving a loose wing interface found on the ground.
component: wing shift bracket (107-100205, spare 107-102843) 1/4-20 threaded holes
failure_mode: threaded holes not tapped through as drawn, so nylon wing bolts bottom out before clamping and the wing stays loose
contributing: vendor (Top Precision) did not tap holes thru all per drawing
no receiving inspection caught it (11 of 133 brackets in stock non-conforming)

evidence.quote: The drawing specifies this as a thru all end condition, but our manufacturer is not tapping the whole hole.
Out of 133 wing shift brackets in inventory, 11 had insufficiently tapped holes.
Vehicle 300 also has a non conforming wing shift bracket:
689 center wing with 695 wing shift bracket (fully threaded) mounted securely.

team_root_cause: JW: Sep 4, 2024 Only failure mode found is insufficiently tapped holes in wing shift bracket. Wing bolts are unable to tighten all the way, leaving wing loosely attached to fuselage. Wing bolts are not too long.
reasoning: Inspection found the 689 and 300 brackets with partially tapped holes, and a swap test showed the 689 center wing mounted securely to a fully threaded 695 bracket but loosely to the 689 and 300 brackets. Retaining washer binding could not be reproduced. The cause is the bracket supplier not tapping the holes through.
notes: The title mentions delamination but nothing in the ticket investigates it. VA-1926 (aluminum to titanium bracket screws for galling) is related but not the cause. The CA tickets VXEP-593/601/602/603/626 were not read.

contributing: procedures did not say to disable OGCS auto connect when the Edge GCS is used

failure_mode: long GCS mission simulation drops the vehicle link, giving mission upload timeouts and a lost comms mission
contributing: operator moved GCS Ethernet cable to the other port in flight, new IP locked out for about 50 s until link timeout (unsupported operation)
VTOL 1.53 not power cycled between flights, stale mcAlt command caused throttle pause at launch
GCS telemetry lag of 20 to 30 s never explained (moved to VXEP-1311, closed for lack of data)

evidence.quote: A software bug in the GCS, can cause the vehicle to disconnect link during long mission simulations which leads to
Data was not in provided logs. Unable to investigate.
I don’t see any mission upload/download timeouts in the debug of the AAR currently attached
Switching Ethernet ports while connected to a vehicle is not a supported operation.
If this is the case, the mcAlt cmd is never reset after the flight, so this explains why the altitude command is high.
We don’t have enough information/diagnostics to investigate further, I’m not sure what the final dispo should be given that.

would_settle_it.what: GCS debug and event logs for the first flight showing the mission upload timeouts and whether the link dropped during the simulation
timing of the GCS freeze versus the lost comms mission popup to match with XComm link timeout entries

The Ethernet reconnect delay is well explained by XComm rebuke and timeout log lines and the throttle pause by an old VTOL firmware behavior. component: GCS Launch Wizard mission check / mission.txt FTP side channel
failure_mode: W1 lost from the launch route after mission checkout, either deleted or corrupted, with no recheck before upload; side channel mission.txt has no integrity check
contributing: Launch Wizard does not rerun mission checkout after edits
link fault during FTP of mission.txt
mission simulation does not flag a single waypoint launch route

evidence.quote: We were unable to determine the exact cause of W1 being deleted in this case, but an errant keypress or mission file corruption are possible explanations.
[09:04:00.660 1273.660] ap link fault: local rx okay ap rx bad
– To support downloading the mission from another GCS, the mission is also uploaded via a side channel which does not
re-loaded the mission on first GCS to see if it was missing from the saved version of the mission (it was).
If the operator deletes W1 after completing the mission checkout page (intentionally or not) the launch wizard will still allow launching the vehicle.

team_view_in_comments: We were unable to determine the exact cause of W1 being deleted in this case, but an errant keypress or mission file corruption are possible explanations.

GCS1 event log key and edit entries between mission checkout and upload

event: VXE 514 (SOFC fuel cell aircraft) overheated on the ground during fuel cell warmup, smoked from the exhaust ports and melted fuel cell nylon parts; no flight.
failure_mode: nose cone fan not moving air although commanded on (supFanEn), so fuselage ambient temperature rose above 100 C during fuel cell warmup
contributing: operator restarted aircraft and fuel cell after fuel cell fault 9360 with no fault description in the GCS
GCS health window and fuel cell control window showed conflicting fault status

evidence.quote: I can observe the fuselage ambient temperature climbing throughout the warmup consistent with the behavior we see without a nose cone fan.
But I do see an indication in the Data (supFanEn) that the AC was attempting to power the nose cone fan throughout the fuel cell warmup.
Heat deformation present on Cathode & Anode suspension, likely occurred due to nosecone fan failure.
Replaced cooling fan, which was damaged by thermal event.

team_root_cause:
Failure or non-operation of the Nose Cone Cooling fan, resulting in lack of active cooling in fuselage during Fuel Cell operation causing overheat. Internal Fuselage temperature reaching temperatures >100degC.
Additionally, without information about specific Fuel Cell Fault, the operators restarted the aircraft after seeing fault 9360, causing the system to melt.

would_settle_it.what: fuselage ambient temperature versus supFanEn and 12 V current to confirm the fan was commanded but drew no current
bench test of the removed nose cone fan and its 12 V connector to see whether the fan, wiring or supply failed

attachments_read: 24467_D4500630 Incoming QC post cooling fan replace.txt.md
reasoning: The log shows the fan commanded on (supFanEn) while fuselage temperature climbed like a no fan case, and the fuel cell fault was excessive board temperature. The fuel cell teardown found heat damage consistent with loss of fuselage cooling and a stack in good health. The removed nose cone fan was never tested, so whether the fan, its wiring or its 12 V supply failed is not shown.
notes: The fuel cell RMA QC logs (D4500630) were scanned by parsing the fault columns rather than read line by line: the first QC run shows FaultCoolingFan code 5248, the post replacement run shows no faults. That cooling fan is the fuel cell's own fan, damaged by the heat, not the aircraft nose cone fan. VXEP-714 (fault code table CA) not read.

event: VXE 444 aborted two launches in a row at about 10 ft after VTOL lift off.
failure_mode: loss of link during launch triggered the designed launch abort
contributing: vehicle on old software v6.1.2
first flight AAR held no vehicle data
range frequency clearance and radios not checked

evidence.quote: [15:54:54.050 410.050] ap dbg: vt lost link during lch, aborting
The first flight AAR didn’t have any data from the vehicle.
The first things to check would be the radios and frequency clearance for the range.

team_root_cause: It is believed to be a software issue but given the lack of data it is hard to determine
disagreement: The Root Cause field says "It is believed to be a software issue", but the only vehicle log line says "vt lost link during lch, aborting" and the closing comment says "Loss of link". The abort worked as designed on a degraded datalink, so the start point is the link, not the software.

would_settle_it.what: XComm link state, RSSI/SNR and GCS side link logs before the abort to tell radio or RF interference from a GCS/network fault

reasoning: The second flight log shows the VTOL autopilot aborting because it lost link during launch, which is the designed response. The first flight had no vehicle data, so the same cause is assumed but not shown. Why the link dropped (radio, frequency interference, GCS) is not in the files.
notes: Two events; only the second has vehicle data.

event: VXE 513 showed repeated magnetometer faults in flight and on landing during a training flight; the aircraft flew normally on fixed wing heading updates.
component: VTOL AP magnetometer health check (CalcImuMagFieldOk in taskOneHz)
failure_mode: taskOneHz did not save floating point context (missing portTASK_USES_FLOATING_POINT), so float locals in the mag check were corrupted on task switch, giving impossible values and a false MAGFAIL
contributing: magmargin threshold printed and applied as 1-margin due to a code bug

evidence.quote: we know the 166 Gauss reading for measured mag field strength is impossible since the range of the sensor’s scaling is 4 Gauss.
Based on the data recorded to the .CSV file there was no excessive mag field.
I made a hack build that moved all the locals to file scope in function CalcImuMagFieldOk(), imu.cpp.
Root cause appears to be a missing call to portTASK_USES_FLOATING_POINT() in taskOneHz.

team_root_cause: Software bug due to lack of FPU support in Mag calc task. This had been found independently and a fix is in v6.4
reasoning: The MAGFAIL entry on 513 holds impossible values (166 Gauss measured, 0.003 Gauss expected) while the recorded mag data and the earlier expected field read were normal, so the fault came from the check, not the sensor. FS2-2097 shows the same signature on the bench, made it go away by moving the float locals out of the task stack, and traced it to the 1 Hz task lacking FPU context saving. The final targeted fix test is not recorded, so confidence is medium.
notes: Open HLB warm up via the XComm page during flight was raised by the reporter but not linked to the fault.

event: After glide landings, the nose cone fan on VXE 600 (and VXE 530) kept running after the fuel cell had cooled below the shutoff temperature, with the battery still connected; no damage.
contributing: both aircraft were glide landed, skipping the normal landing state machine transitions
AAR data ends before fuel cell temperature fell below the fan shutoff threshold
aircraft on older autopilot firmware; customer did not see it again on AP FW 6.05p

evidence.quote: He notes and acknowledges that the batteries were connected during this anomaly.
This flight appears to have been glide landed, this may lead to a bug in the state machine resulting in the fan not being turned off.
The captured AAR ends before the temp drops below the threshold to turn off the fan.
The command to shut down the fan does come from the autopilot though so if the autopilot is powered down and the fuel cell is still running that would explain why the fan doesn’t shut down.
I don’t recall the fan staying on after the fuel cell cooled down after multiple flights 3 weeks ago using AP FW 6.05p

team_root_cause: Suspected Operator Error. Fuel Cell cannot operate Nose Cone Fan without connected to battery at described temperature/operation state as there are no other sources of power on aircraft. Possible partial disconnect of the battery by removing VTOL Harness (from center wing) and not Avionics/Fuel Cell/Nose Cone Fan harness (from Fuselage).
disagreement: The Root Cause field blames a partial battery disconnect, but the customer later clarified "He notes and acknowledges that the batteries were connected during this anomaly." Later engineering review suspected the glide landing state machine or avionics powered down first, and said the AAR "ends before the temp drops below the threshold to turn off the fan", so no cause is shown.

would_settle_it.what: later XComm log segments covering the period when reactor temperature fell below 150 C with the fan still on, to show fan command and autopilot state

reasoning: The first report assumed the battery was disconnected, which the customer later corrected. Engineers then suspected the glide landing path through the state machine, but code review said FS_LANDED should still turn the fan off, and no log covers the time the fan stayed on. Without that data the cause does not get past the symptom.
notes: Covers two aircraft (600 main, 530 also). Closed as Cannot Reproduce and added to the Bermuda Triangle list. RMA-459 attachments (quotes for SD card work) not read as not cause related.

event: VXE 574 at 29 Palms turned hard right away from the PLZ after VTOL motors started on landing, then could only fly backwards until the operator aborted, and the aircraft was damaged in an unintended landing.
failure_mode: known landing abort bug triggered by a lift system power fault, itself apparently from bad VTOL IMU sensor data, causing loss of control in VTOL
contributing: mismatched and outdated SW/FW (GCS 6.1.2, XComm 4.60, FWAP 6.05m, VTOL 1.44) with ADs for 6.2.9 and 6.3.4 not applied
VTOL AP IP configured as tail number 1
bad VTOL IMU sensor data

evidence.quote: Root cause is known landing abort bug triggered by power fault which seems to be caused by bad IMU sensor data on VTOL.
This vehicle is also misconfigured, the SW/FW images do not match.
VTOL AP IP wasn’t configured per the tail number (was configured as tail number 1).
System faults were able to trigger autopilot commanded land aborts that were not allowed to complete. This led to
VXEP-598 (VXE-574) – Aircraft made hard right turn from PLZ during VTOL landing

team_root_cause:
Operator Error: Misconfigured SW/FW versions
Loss of control caused by known land abort bug (triggered by lift system power fault, likely caused by IMU sensor)

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP logs around the landing: the power fault flag, IMU data and land abort state to confirm the trigger chain
Jason Scherer's VXEP-598 investigation report with the flight timeline

reasoning: The aircraft ran outdated VTOL 1.44 firmware with mismatched versions and missing ADs. The engineer who reviewed the downloaded VTOL logs states the loss of control came from a known landing abort bug triggered by a lift system power fault tied to bad IMU data, fixed in 6.3.4. The log excerpts themselves are not in the files and the IMU fault was not confirmed by hardware test, so this is narrowed to the VTOL software path with medium confidence.
notes: Comments on 2024-12-05 briefly said the downloaded data was from 594, then retracted. The RMA intake PDF has no extractable text. The two AD PDFs on FS2-2321 were searched for abort, landing, power fault and IMU text rather than read line by line; the 6.3.4 AD describes the partial land abort fix.
